briefing.text: SCLC subtypes (SCLC-A, SCLC-N, SCLC-P, and SCLC-Y) are defined by RNA or protein (IHC) expression levels of the transcription factors ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3 (and YAP1). DNA mutations or copy-number changes do not define them. Before analysing, search every file, including the commented clinical headers, for any expression, IHC or subtype variable (e.g. grep -i 'ASCL1|NEUROD1|POU2F3|YAP1|SUBTYPE|EXPRESSION|IHC'). Then base the label on what variables actually exist and what they show.
briefing.reason: The choice of label depends on whether a variable that defines the subtype exists in these tables. The teams need to know which kind of variable defines a subtype before they choose what to analyse.

briefing.text: If ASCL1, NEUROD1 or POU2F3 has no mutations or CNAs, that does not mean the subtype is absent, because subtype depends on expression level and not on alterations. These genes may also not be on the MSK-IMPACT panels used. Use data_gene_panel_matrix.txt, the row names in data_cna.txt and Hugo_Symbol in data_mutations.txt to check whether each gene was measured at all. A gene that was not measured counts as unmeasured, not as absent.
briefing.reason: This prevents a common mistake: reading 'no calls' as 'subtype not present'.

briefing.text: Genomic proxies such as MYC amplification (linked to SCLC-N) or MYCL amplification (linked to SCLC-A) are statistical associations, not subtype definitions. For example, MYC amplification also occurs in SCLC-P/Y. SCLC is genetically homogeneous (near-universal TP53/RB1 loss), and studies have found no DNA-defined subtypes. If you look at these proxies, report them only as indirect hints and do not base the label on them.
briefing.reason: The CNA data make proxy-based subtype inference tempting, and these proxies are unreliable.

briefing.text: Published SCLC PDX/CDX biobanks report models with high ASCL1, NEUROD1 and POU2F3 expression, based on RNA-seq and IHC. That is prior knowledge, not evidence from these tables. Choose the label only from variables and results in the provided files, not from what you recall of the literature.
briefing.reason: This keeps the answer tied to this dataset and stops literature recall from replacing data analysis.

briefing.text: In data_clinical_sample.txt (the header is the first line not starting with '#'), SAMPLE_CLASS separates PDX, CDX (CTC/blood-derived) and possibly patient tumour samples. Tabulate SAMPLE_CLASS, PROCEDURE_TYPE and TISSUE_SITE. The hypothesis concerns only PDX/CDX models, so restrict any subtype-related analysis to those rows. Serial models from the same PATIENT_ID are not independent.
briefing.reason: This defines the correct population for the hypothesis and helps avoid double counting.

briefing.text: SCLC models can be mixed-subtype or heterogeneous (for example ASCL1/NEUROD1 co-expression, or subtype switching across passages or after treatment). If any expression-like variable exists, look at continuous levels per model rather than a single exclusive call per model. A subtype counts as present if its TF is clearly expressed in any model.
briefing.reason: This only matters if an expression-like variable is found. In that case it changes how presence is judged.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume transcriptional subtypes can only be assigned from RNA/IHC data for ASCL1/NEUROD1/POU2F3 and that no DNA-level proxy in these tables is acceptable evidence; neither tested whether any proxy relationship is observable in the data.

Both teams treated all 42 SAMPLE_CLASS=PDX rows (including 8 Blood Draw CDX) as the in-scope model set without checking histology (CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED includes combined SCLC, LCNEC and lung neuroendocrine tumour).
unused_evidence: YAP1 is present as a row in data_cna.txt (the fourth proposed SCLC subtype regulator); team A grepped for it but neither team reported what its presence means for the hypothesis, which names only three regulators.
CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED shows non-pure-SCLC histologies (4 combined SCLC, 1 LCNEC, 1 lung NET) among samples; neither team used it to define scope.
Paired Tumor vs PDX samples from the same patient (27 Tumor rows) were tabulated but not used; they cannot supply subtype information either, so unlikely to change the label.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named indirect genomic inference (e.g. MYC-family amplification) as their weakest point and dismissed it by argument rather than by showing whether any subtype-linked gene alteration is even measured on the panels used.

Neither team confirmed from the gene panel definitions whether ASCL1, NEUROD1 and POU2F3 are absent because they were not targeted or because they were targeted and unaltered; team A asserts 'not measured' but the gene panel matrix gives only panel names.
second_readings: The hypothesis could be read as a claim about the genes being altered or measured in the models rather than about expression-defined subtypes; under that reading, absence from the targeted panel still leaves the claim untestable rather than supported.
'PDX/CDX models' could be read as only the PDX/CDX rows, or as the patients from whom the models were derived (including matched Tumor samples); neither reading adds a subtype variable.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed 'Not verifiable' fairly strongly: the data are DNA panel sequencing plus clinical tables with no expression, IHC or subtype variable, and the three named regulators are not in the genomic tables. Remaining risks are scope (histology) and whether the genes were untargeted vs unaltered, neither of which seems likely to flip the label.

questions.question: Is there an accepted method to assign SCLC molecular subtypes (ASCL1/NEUROD1/POU2F3/YAP1) from DNA-only targeted sequencing data such as copy-number or mutation profiles, without RNA or protein data?
questions.why: Both teams dismissed genomic proxies by argument; an established DNA-based classifier would undermine the 'no relevant variable' conclusion.

findings.question: Are the transcription-factor genes ASCL1, NEUROD1 and POU2F3 included in the gene lists of the MSK-IMPACT targeted sequencing panels (341, 410, 468 gene versions)?
findings.answer: No. None of ASCL1, NEUROD1 or POU2F3 is on IMPACT-341, IMPACT-410 or IMPACT-468. A supplementary table that splits the genes into those on all three versions, on 410+468 only, and on 468 only does not list any of them, and neither does a full 468-gene list. YAP1 is on all three versions. All 341 genes are also in the 410 panel. So when these three genes are missing from the genomic tables, it means they were never measured, not that they were measured and found unaltered.

findings.question: Is there an accepted method to assign SCLC molecular subtypes (ASCL1/NEUROD1/POU2F3/YAP1) from DNA-only targeted sequencing data such as copy-number or mutation profiles, without RNA or protein data?
findings.answer: No accepted method works from mutation or copy-number data. The subtypes are defined by how strongly the transcription factors are expressed, measured by RNA or IHC (Rudin et al. 2019). Chemi et al. 2022 (Nature Cancer) state explicitly that genomic profiling (CNAs and somatic mutations) has not mapped to the TF-based subtypes. The only DNA-based subtyping methods are DNA-methylation classifiers: cfDNA T7-MBD-seq (Chemi 2022) and an RRBS-based classifier (Heeke et al. Cancer Cell 2024). These need methylation data, which MSK-IMPACT mutation, CNA, seg and SV tables do not contain.
